content_metadata.description: An interview with Dr. Ludwig Aigner hosted by Tracy Weslosky, discussing the potential of drug repurposing for brain rejuvenation, focusing on the asthma drug Montelukast.

qAndA.answer: Dr. Aigner is a specialist in age rejuvenation and brain rejuvenation.
qAndA.question: What is Dr. Aigner's primary area of expertise?

qAndA.answer: Drug repurposing offers a more cost-effective and time-efficient way to develop new treatments compared to creating entirely new drugs.
qAndA.question: Why is drug repurposing gaining traction in the pharmaceutical industry?

qAndA.answer: Montelukast is approved for the treatment of asthma.
qAndA.question: What is the primary indication for which Montelukast is currently approved?

qAndA.answer: Effective drug delivery to the brain is crucial because the blood-brain barrier poses a challenge for many drugs to reach their target in the brain.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of drug delivery in the context of repurposing drugs for brain diseases?

qAndA.answer: IntelGenx specializes in improving the pharmacokinetic properties of drugs, making them more effectively available to the body, which is crucial for repurposing drugs for brain diseases.
qAndA.question: What is IntelGenx's specific expertise that makes them a suitable partner for this project?

mood.description: Curious - The interview format and discussion of a novel scientific approach contribute to a feeling of interest and inquiry.

narrativeProgression.description: Tracy introduces Dr. Aigner as an expert in brain rejuvenation.
Dr. Aigner explains the shift in focus from protecting neurons to actively rejuvenating the aging brain.
The conversation transitions to the concept of drug repurposing as a cost-effective and innovative strategy.
Dr. Aigner highlights the potential of Montelukast, an asthma drug, for brain rejuvenation.
The discussion then delves into the critical role of drug delivery in repurposing, particularly for brain diseases.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Today I have the pleasure of speaking with Dr. Ludwig Agner.
How are you today?
Great, thanks very much.
It is a real pleasure to meet you.
You're a age rejuvenation specialist and neuroscientist that's recently joined Intel
Genics' Scientific Board.
Can you tell us a little bit more about what you do?
Well, I'm a neuroscientist working since 2025 years on regeneration, brain regeneration,
more lately focusing more on rejuvenation.
So that goes beyond, let's say, the last, you know, the attempts of the last tech heads
where people just try to protect neurons from dying.
Now we are looking at the aged brain because aging is the main risk factor for many of the
diseases that we are interested in, for example, dementia, Alzheimer's dementia.
So we would like to go beyond just protecting neurons from dying, but we would really like
to make the old, the aged brain younger, with other words, really try to rejuvenate the
aged brain with the aim, basically, to finally also develop therapies for dementia for Alzheimer
and so on.
Okay, this is a very exciting industry and I'll tell you, my brain could use some work
here.
So in particular, you speak a lot about drug repurposing, the drug delivery in drug repurposing.
For some of our investors out there that may not be familiar with this, can you tell us
a little bit more about what this means?
The drug repurposing is also, let's say, innovative and very young way to come up with
new drugs for certain diseases, new drugs, meaning the new use for already known drugs.
Now, if you just look at the costs of drugs to be developed, any kind of completely new
drug would cost, I mean, these days something like $2.6 billion for each individual drug.
So these are huge costs.
Now, if you are able to use a drug that has been already developed and used for a certain
disease and you find that this drug might be also useful for another disease, you just
take this drug and develop it for this new disease, for this new indication that you are
interested in and that's kind of what repurposing is or repositioning is also called.
So looking at IntellGenux's website, the company is very focused on Monteloucast, which
is used for the treatment of asthma.
Can you tell us a little bit more about this?
Well, Monteloucast has been is already approved and it's on the market since more than 15
years for the use for its use in asthma.
That's what it has been developed for.
Now, we found out sort of through our, you know, basic scientific work that things that
happen basically in asthmatic patients in the lung are also present, so the molecular
signolings that are present there.
They are also, we find them also in the brain of aged people, of aged, along aging and
these signoling mechanisms are already there in brains of neurodegenerative diseases.
So basically we sort of found that what is happening in the lung with asthmatic patients
is also happening in the age brain.
So that's why we sort of came up with the idea of if we are able to block this and Monteloucast
actually does that, that's what it has been developed for in the field of asthma.
So if we block these same signolings and signaling molecules and mechanisms in the brain,
we might actually be able to rejuvenate the brain or to make the brain younger and to
block these signoling mechanisms.
So if I understand you correctly, until Gen X is working with Monteloucast, they're
looking at the drug repurposing options that you have and it looks like it might be used
for age or jubination of the brain, is that correct?
Yes, that's correct, absolutely right.
So reviewing Intel Gen X's website, obviously drug delivery may have an impact in the
drug repurposing, is that correct and can you explain that a little bit better?
Yes, absolutely.
I mean, you know, many drugs have been for example developed for a certain disease and even
though this drug might work for another in another disease, you still, especially when
we are talking about brain diseases, you still need to improve for example this drug in terms
of its pharmacokinetic.
So can we can we can we make this drug better, for example, available to the brain, can
we make it better so that the pharmacokinetic sort of the speed and the amount of drug that
really enters the body, can we improve that?
And that's basically sort of what we are trying with Intel Gen X because they are specialist
in especially that field.
So that's why we teamed up with Intel Gen X.
Well thank you so much Dr. Agner for joining us today and we look forward to your
two follow-ups with you to see how this is going.
Thank you very much.

youtube_description:
IntelGenX Technologies Corp. (TSXV: IGX | OTCQX: IGXT) is a pioneer in innovative drug delivery technologies addressing unmet medical and commercial needs. Established in 2003, the Montreal-based company develops innovations in pharmaceutical delivery based on its proprietary drug formulation technologies, VersaFilmTM, VersaTabTM, and AdVersaTM. The company's goal is to be the first choice for oral solid dose innovation.

IntelGenX is now in the forefront of addressing rejuvenating the brain in the aged to combat degenerative disorders such as dementia and Alzheimer's. A team recently demonstrated that the anti-asthmatic drug Montelukast structurally and functionally rejuvenates the aged brain.

May 11, 2016: InvestorIntel publisher Tracy Weslosky Interviews Ludwig Aigner, a member of IntelGenX's Scientific Advisory Board. Dr Aigner has been working on spinal cord and brain rejuvenation over a 25-year period. He explains
◾How research is going beyond just slowly the brain's aging
◾Why existing drugs could be re-purposed to improve brain functions — and save huge developmental costs

Tracy Weslosky: It is a real pleasure to meet you. You’re an age rejuvenation specialist, a neuroscientist that’s recently joined IntelGenX’s scientific board. Can you tell us a little bit more about what you do?

Now we are looking at the aged brain because aging is the main risk factor for many of the diseases that we’re interested in, for example, dementia, Alzheimer’s dementia. We would like to go beyond just protecting neurons from dying, but we would really like to make the old — the aged brain — younger. In other words, really try to rejuvenate the aged brain with aim basically to finally also develop therapies for dementia, for Alzheimer’s and so on.
